source_text: Illud tamen admoneo, solere etiam te in scriptis tuis tenebras non dicere creaturam, sed absentia luminis remanere obscuritatem; ut nihil aliud sit obtenebratio, quam splendoris exclusio. Quod ergo excluditur, creaturam vocas; quod remanet, tenebras; quod quidem vulgatum a philosophis est; nec nunc quaero verumne esse putetur, an falsum; sed illud inculco, tenebras tu non dicis esse aliud quam nihil; in homine autem, id est, opere Dei malum ideo exstitisse argumentaris, quia de nihilo factus erat; causam ergo mali illud nihilum fuisse confirmas, quod nihilum tenebras etiam pronuntias. Necessitatem itaque mali de tenebrarum dicis conditione descendere. Igitur nec in hoc a praeceptore dissentis, quoniam voluntatem malam pariter aeternis tenebris deputatis.
pass_a_gloss: That nevertheless I advise, that even you are accustomed in your writings not to say darkness is a creature, but that obscurity remains by the absence of light; so that darkening is nothing other than an exclusion of splendor. What therefore is excluded, you call a creature; what remains, darkness; which indeed has been published by the philosophers; nor do I now ask whether it is thought true or false; but I impress this, that you do not say darkness is other than nothing; but in the human, that is in a work of God, you argue that evil existed therefore, because he had been made from nothing; you confirm therefore that that nothing was the cause of evil, which nothing you also pronounce darkness. You say therefore that a necessity of evil descends from the condition of darkness. Therefore not even in this do you dissent from the teacher, since you equally assign an evil will to eternal darkness.

pass_b_english: I point out, however, that in your writings you too habitually say darkness is not a creature, but that obscurity remains through the absence of light: darkening is nothing other than the exclusion of brightness. What is excluded you call a creature; what remains you call darkness. This view is indeed widespread among philosophers. I am not now asking whether it should be regarded as true or false. I press this point: you say darkness is nothing other than nothing. Yet you argue that evil arose in a human being, God’s work, because he was made from nothing. You therefore affirm that this nothing was evil’s cause, and you also call this nothing darkness. You thus say the necessity of evil descends from the condition of darkness. Even in this you do not differ from your teacher, since both of you attribute an evil will to eternal darkness.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian contrasts opportunity/help with imposed necessity; load-bearing against natural compulsion to sin.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
